items.text: FALL TEMPS TO RING IN THE ‘BER’ MONTH📉🍂🌧️❄️a notable pattern change is setting up across the Pacific Northwest and parts of the West, moving into the first week of September, bringing cooler temperatures and increased chances for precipitation! The main driver is a trough developing near the West Coast. This southward dip in the jet stream will be associated with cooler air aloft and lower atmospheric pressure, favoring cooler air being drawn southward into the region. The latest numerical guidance continues to show the Pacific Northwest has increased odds of below-normal temperatures with the cooler signal extending south through parts of the western Great Basin and into northern and central California. The trough will also strengthen onshore flow from the Pacific, allowing cooler, moisture-rich marine air to move inland. Chances for above-normal precipitation are elevated across parts of the West, with the Pacific Northwest favored to see wetter than normal conditions. This doesn't necessarily mean continuous rain or that every location will see significant rainfall. Rather, the overall pattern becomes more favorable for passing weather systems, showers and periods of wetter weather compared with what is typical. The increased cloud cover, precipitation and stronger marine influence should also help reinforce the cooler pattern. There’s also a chance for mountain snow for the Northwest. Meanwhile, it's almost the opposite story farther south and east. Strong ridging is expected to favor continued above-normal temperatures across much of the Southwest and Southern Plains📉🌧️❄️

It's been fifteen years since Hurricane Irene made landfall as a strong Category 1 Hurricane near Cape Lookout, but the impacts from Irene are still apparent in parts of the Outer Banks in Dare and Hyde Counties, from altered land and infrastructure. 

The most iconic and disruptive impact was the storm surge from Pamlico Sound that crashed over the narrow strip of land on the Southern Outer Banks, tearing open multiple new inlets on Hatteras Island (including a massive 200+ foot breach at the Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge). This would effectively cut off Hatteras Island from the rest of the world. The roughly 2,500 residents on Hatteras Island were temporarily stranded, requiring emergency ferry service to deliver supplies and personnel. Impacts are still felt today on Pea Island. Over 800 homes and businesses on Ocracoke Island were flooded, and nearly 30% of all homes in Pamlico County were flooded. 15.74 inches of rain fell in Bayboro, and tropical storm-force winds extended over 200 miles from the center of Irene thanks to its large size. Half a million folks lost power. 

Do you remember Irene?

Tropical Storm Dolly formed earlier today, but it’s likely to be a short-lived system. Dolly will run into a wall of strong wind shear this weekend, which should quickly take its toll.

Fall is just around the corner, but if you're in Central Florida, don't expect it to arrive quickly. 

I know the appearance of Halloween decorations in stores, PSLs & everything else pumpkin makes it seem like fall is just around the corner. 

Although meteorological fall is Sept, Oct & Nov, here in the Bay Area, we don't really start to feel "fall" until the month of October. Even then, it's really the second half of October that starts to see more noticeable reductions in temperatures & humidity levels. Highs in October usually stay in the 80s.

The real cool stuff, highs in the 70s, doesn't happen until November & lasts through the winter months. 

Until then, September doesn't usually see much, if any, "fall-like" weather, though a drop in the humidity later in the month is not unheard of, which can at least lead to cooler nights & mornings.

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: TROPICAL STORM ISELLE BRINGS MOISTURE TO CALIFORNIA BEGINNING TODAY🌀🌴🌧️ ⛈️a plume of deep tropical and subtropical moisture associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Iselle are being pulled northward into California today and especially Friday as an upper-level trough approaches the West Coast! While this is not expected to be a widespread rain event, moisture levels will increase considerably and scattered showers and storms could develop across portions of the state. Today, tropical moisture begins spreading into Central and Southern California. There is around a low to medium chance for showers across portions of Southern California, the Central Coast and Bay Area while isolated activity will also be possible farther inland. Most locations will remain dry, but brief showers, sprinkles or virga could develop almost anywhere beneath the moisture plume. Thunderstorm chances today remain low but non-zero. The combination of tropical moisture, heat and instability means an isolated heavier shower or thunderstorm cannot be completely ruled out today. Gusty and erratic winds could also occur near showers or virga. The better opportunity for precipitation arrives Friday as the approaching Pacific Northwest trough taps directly into the subtropical moisture plume. Shower chances expand northward into the Sacramento Valley where much of the Valley now has a low to medium chance for rain showers. The Sierra Nevada should have the best opportunity for meaningful precipitation with thunderstorm probabilities increasing Friday. Localized flooding is possible in the Sierra Nevada. This is a classic low-probability, potentially higher-impact setup. Most Californians probably won't see measurable rain, but any isolated thunderstorm that develops within this unusually moist and unstable environment could produce locally heavier rain, lightning and gusty winds🌀🌴🌧️ ⛈️

items.author: MattDevittWeather
items.text:
#BREAKING: Tropical Storm #Dolly has formed in the Atlantic, 4th named storm of the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season. It's currently forecast to be short-lived. Here's the latest and what to know: 

1) Dolly was able to develop from a small window of favorable conditions, but it looks like that will quickly be coming to an end Friday into the weekend as it encounters drier air and increasing wind shear.  More shear and dry air the better…it hurts tropical systems! The official NHC (National Hurricane Center) forecast calls for this to move into the Caribbean and then dissapate / fall apart after. 

2) Over the past several days, I’ve been discussing two track possibilities from the models. Scenario #1 quickly develops a stronger system and has it turning north out to sea. Scenario #2 is a system that either struggles after developing, or never actually develops, and heads more west as a result. Recently, almost all models have been leaning toward the western track, Scenario #2. 

3) The more west it goes, land enters into the mix. First up will be the Caribbean. Leeward Islands and Puerto Rico by Sunday into Monday. Hispaniola by Monday into Tuesday. Then after the Bahamas? Cuba? The United States? All possibilities, but what will it be at that point? Even if it develops and then falls apart, some models indicate the leftovers could try to reorganize over warmer water, greater tropical moisture and lower shear. Not a guarantee, but possible down the road. Best-case scenario is an undeveloped rainmaker. 

4)Thankfully, this is nothing to stress over this early, just putting it on your radar and keeping tabs on it. 

I'll continue to keep you updated 24/7 with no hype, just the facts. Thanks everyone!

items.author: ericsnitilwx
items.text:
TONIGHT IS THE NIGHT! A deep partial lunar eclipse will grace our skies overnight. While not quite a total, it'll be darn close and visually very similar as much of the Moon takes on a deep red hue as it passes into Earth's shadow(s). Earth casts two shadows, a dark umbra and a lighter penumbra where light is only partially blocked. 

These are important distinctions as the penumbral portion of a lunar eclipse is largely underwhelming. The Moon gets a little darker. It's hard to tell and difficult to argue it's worth your time unless you're documenting the entirety of the event. During the partial phase, The Moon enters the umbra, which in turn causes more and more of the Moon to turn deep red. 

Why red if it's hidden in shadow? Light passing around the Earth through the edge of our atmosphere gets scattered. Blues and violets scatter while longer wavelengths of light like red and orange pass through. A small component of these reds bend back toward the Moon. It's akin to projecting every sunrise and sunset onto the Moon's surface, which is why the moniker "Blood Moon" resonates. 

Because this is not quite (but very close) to a total, a small sliver of the Moon's surface will remain white. I'd argue this will be even more photogenic and lovely than totality as the contrast in color is more striking. I hope you're able to see it!

TROPICS | The area of low pressure in the Eastern Atlantic got better organized overnight & the NHC has increased its chance for development to 70%.

items.text: TROPICAL STORM ISELLE INCREASES CALIFORNIA T-STORM CHANCES THURSDAY AND FRIDAY THIS WEEK🌀🌴🌧️ ⛈️a plume of deep tropical and subtropical moisture associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Iselle will be pulled northward into California Thursday and especially Friday as an upper-level trough approaches the West Coast! While this is not expected to be a widespread rain event, moisture levels will increase considerably and scattered showers and storms could develop across portions of the state. On Thursday, tropical moisture begins spreading into Central and Southern California. There is around a low to medium chance for showers across portions of Southern California, the Central Coast and Bay Area while isolated activity will also be possible farther inland. Most locations will remain dry, but brief showers, sprinkles or virga could develop almost anywhere beneath the moisture plume. Thunderstorm chances Thursday remain low but non-zero. The combination of tropical moisture, heat and instability means an isolated heavier shower or thunderstorm cannot be completely ruled out Thursday. Gusty and erratic winds could also occur near showers or virga. The better opportunity for precipitation arrives Friday as the approaching Pacific Northwest trough taps directly into the subtropical moisture plume. Shower chances expand northward into the Sacramento Valley where much of the Valley now has a low to medium chance for rain showers. The Sierra Nevada should have the best opportunity for meaningful precipitation with thunderstorm probabilities increasing Friday. Localized flooding is possible in the Sierra Nevada. This is a classic low-probability, potentially higher-impact setup.  Most Californians probably won't see measurable rain, but any isolated thunderstorm that develops within this unusually moist and unstable environment could produce locally heavier rain, lightning and gusty winds🌀🌴🌧️ ⛈️
